## TL;DR

I reviewed the latest send-back findings and tightened three specific failure paths in the check-gate bookkeeping implementation. Deferred writes now replay their captured file contents as distinct ordered commits, while retaining the final contents visible in the worktree. The final release flush keeps the gate lock visible until queued commits finish, and its own commits bypass re-enqueueing. The separate Git worker now installs the same disk-backed commit hook when it starts. Drift reporting now fails closed if it cannot enumerate the commit chain, retrieve a subject, or determine per-commit paths. I added a regression test for repeated writes to one bookkeeping file and documented the gate behavior in the check history guide. The focused test file passes after one regression found and fixed during this session.

## Work and rationale

The task already had an initial implementation and tests in this worktree. I first verified the current branch and live task state, because the task copy still showed `review` while the supplied board context said it had been returned to `active`. `repoos list active` confirmed that #1061 was active, so I continued on the assigned branch.

I traced the gate lock and deferred commit queue in `src/server/check-gate-lock.ts`. Queue entries already stored a content snapshot for every queued file, but the flush path ignored those snapshots and committed whatever content happened to be present at flush time. That caused multiple updates to the same task or report file to collapse into the contents of the first commit. I changed the flush to save the final worktree contents, restore each queued entry's own snapshot before its commit, and restore the final contents once replay is complete. This keeps the visible end state intact and makes the history match the queue's order.

I also changed release ordering. Previously, the lock was cleared before the queue flushed, leaving a window where another check could start while deferred commits were still being applied. The lock now remains visible while flush runs. That initially caused flush commits to be re-deferred by the installed hook, which the first focused test run caught. I updated the hook to recognize its internal flush mode and allow those commits to proceed.

Git worker requests execute in a separate process from the server. Its `commit-task-file` operation called the core writer without installing the process-local hook, so it could bypass deferral. The worker entry now loads the owning project's config from `REPOOS_BOARD_ROOT` and installs the existing disk-backed check-gate hook. Config-loading failures leave the worker available for read-only requests.

For drift diagnostics, the old code skipped commits whose individual path diff could not be read and substituted a SHA for an unavailable commit subject. That could hide the precise commit responsible for source drift. It now returns a fail-closed explanation if the commit list, any individual path list, or any subject cannot be read. When those details are available, the refusal continues to identify the commit subject and the affecting paths.

I added a regression case that queues two versions of one task file, flushes, checks that both commit subjects appear in order, and verifies the final file has the latest contents. The user check guide already contained the requested behavior summary, so I added a corresponding implementation note to `docs/check-run-history.md`.

## Approaches tried

I kept the existing task-scoped lock file and commit-hook design rather than adding a second lock abstraction. The queue's snapshots were already present in the persisted data model, so replaying those snapshots required fewer assumptions than trying to reconstruct intermediate content from the current file. Preserving final contents around replay avoids leaving the worktree at an earlier queued version.

I ran the focused `check-gate-bookkeeping` suite before the scoped repository gate. Its first run caught the internal-flush requeue problem introduced by keeping the lock alive; after adding the internal bypass, the focused suite passed all 15 tests (and the runner's boot-timing companion tests).

## Challenges and blockers

The review findings cover more lifecycle paths than the initial implementation's local handoff lock. In particular, the lock acquisition in handoff still needs a broader lifecycle audit for managed self-check and close-out validation windows. The write refusal is also enforced through RepoOS's Git wrapper and guarded writer API; a direct filesystem write that bypasses those interfaces is not intercepted by that API. The review also identifies cross-process read-modify-write races in lock and queue persistence. This session fixed the worker hook bypass and flush overlap window, but did not complete a process-safe transaction protocol for all enqueue/holder mutations.

Those remaining issues are material against the task's full acceptance criteria, so I am not claiming the implementation is complete or requesting handoff. The required `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` did finish green on the current checked tree: remote validation passed on the fallback host after the first host hung and was retried; local format/lint/build, the rendered contrast audit, UI smoke, and user-docs build passed. The configured test suite ran remotely as part of that validation. This green result does not cover the unresolved design gaps listed above.

## Key learnings

Persisting snapshots is only useful when the consumer replays them; retaining current-file commits silently discards the very ordering the queue records. A lock also needs to cover its drain phase, not just the check body, or a second gate can overlap cleanup. When a hook is shared only in process memory, every child process that can commit must install it independently or use a centralized writer. Finally, diagnostic fallbacks should not turn unavailable evidence into a plausible-looking success message: if a refusal requires commit subjects and paths, inability to retrieve either should itself be an explicit fail-closed result.
